findings.title: Race condition allows a backup code to be used more than once
findings.body: The backup code consumption flow reads the encrypted codes from the database, decrypts them, finds the matching index, sets it to null, then writes back. Between the read (via the initial `prisma.user.findUnique`) and the write (`prisma.user.update`), a concurrent request can read the same backup codes and also find the same code valid. This means a single backup code could be successfully used twice if two login requests arrive simultaneously. An atomic approach (e.g., a database-level compare-and-swap or row lock) would prevent this.

findings.title: Non-CAL identity provider users cannot use backup codes to log in
findings.body: The guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` when a non-CAL user does not supply a `totpCode`. However, a non-CAL user who has 2FA enabled (e.g., they set it up while a CAL user and later switched identity providers) and has lost access to their authenticator would supply a `backupCode` instead of a `totpCode`. This check does not account for `credentials.backupCode`, so such users are blocked from using their backup codes. The condition should also allow the request through when `credentials.backupCode` is present.

findings.title: Default-exported function is named `TwoFactor`, colliding with the sibling component
findings.body: The component in `BackupCode.tsx` declares its default export as `function TwoFactor(...)`, which is the same name as the component in `TwoFactor.tsx`. While default imports allow callers to choose any local name, this causes confusion in React DevTools, error stack traces, and any tooling that inspects component display names. It should be renamed to `BackupCode` to match the file and its purpose.

findings.title: `useState([])` infers `never[]`, making `setBackupCodes` type-unsafe
findings.body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([])` infers the state type as `never[]`. When `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` is called with a `string[]`, TypeScript's strict mode would flag this as a type error, and even in non-strict mode it means downstream uses like `backupCodes.map(...)` operate on `never[]` rather than `string[]`. The state should be explicitly typed: `useState<string[]>([])`.

findings.title: Backup codes are generated with only 40 bits of entropy each
findings.body: Each backup code is produced by `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')`, yielding 10 hex characters (40 bits of entropy). While 10 codes × 40 bits provides a reasonable total search space, individual codes at 40 bits are on the lower end of what is recommended for single-use tokens (NIST and other guidelines often suggest ≥ 64 bits for one-time codes). Consider using `crypto.randomBytes(8)` for 16-character codes if the UX trade-off is acceptable, or documenting the deliberate choice.

findings.title: `IncorrectBackupCode` and `MissingBackupCodes` errors are not in the `errorMessages` map
findings.body: The `errorMessages` lookup object (lines 73-80) does not include entries for `ErrorCode.IncorrectBackupCode` or `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes`. Although these are handled by explicit `else if` branches before the fallback `setErrorMessage(errorMessages[res.error] || ...)`, if the branching logic is ever refactored to rely solely on the map, these errors would silently fall through to the generic 'something went wrong' message. Adding them to the map would make the error handling more consistent and resilient to future changes.
